extracted.intended_audience: constitutional designers, statesmen, political theorists, and students of government
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for structuring representative institutions (bicameral legislatures, the executive, appointment and responsibility, and advisory councils) in a democratic constitution. Focuses on what makes effective checks, responsible administration, and suitable composition of high offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited value of a Second Chamber as a check on an otherwise unchecked democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: “I set little value on any check which a Second Chamber can apply to a democracy otherwise unchecked; and ... it is of comparatively little importance whether the Parliament consists of two Chambers or only of one.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'all other constitutional questions are rightly decided' a Second Chamber adds little; the practical utility of a second house depends on the broader constitutional context rather than its mere existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of similarly composed bicameral houses
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are two chambers of similar composition, both will obey the same influences, and whatever has a majority in one of the houses will be likely to have it in the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement of consent of both houses may delay measures but usually only delays marginal majorities; the main consequence may be short delay or the opportunity to appeal to electors. Duplicate composition provides little independent check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two chambers as a check against undivided power / to promote conciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: The consideration which tells most, in my judgment, in favor of two Chambers ... is the evil effect produced upon the mind of any holder of power ... by the consciousness of having only themselves to consult. ... One of the most indispensable requisites ... is conciliation; a readiness to compromise; ... the mutual give and take between two houses is a perpetual school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second chamber can temper majoritarian despotism by forcing deliberation, compromise, and habitual conciliation; its practical value is in cultivating moderation and preventing the corrupting influence of undivided power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy of a dissimilar Second Chamber depends on external social support
rubrics_metrics.description: An assembly which does not rest on the basis of some great power in the country is ineffectual against one which does. An aristocratic House is only powerful in an aristocratic state of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second chamber intended to restrain a democratic majority must have social forces outside the legislature to back it; without a social base its resistance will be ineffective and may provoke general opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Chamber should act 'in and through' the democratic House rather than in open opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: It can only act to advantage by not holding itself apart, and compelling every one to declare himself either with or against it, but taking a position among the crowd rather than in opposition to it, and drawing to itself the elements most capable of allying themselves with it on any given point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moderating chamber should work as an integrating influence within the democratic polity (infusing its leaven into the mass), not as a separate antagonistic body that provokes a rally against it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best character of a Second Chamber: represent elements exempt from class prejudices yet not offensive to democratic feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The best constitution of a Second Chamber is that which embodies the greatest number of elements exempt from the class interests and prejudices of the majority, but having in themselves nothing offensive to democratic feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for membership that is independent of majority class interests yet acceptable to democratic sensibilities; main tempering power still rests in the popular House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition by public-service and tested merit (the 'Chamber of Statesmen' ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one House represents popular feeling, the other should represent personal merit, tested and guaranteed by actual public service, and fortified by practical experience. ... such a Senate might include: members of a Legislative Commission, chief justices, puisne judges of five years, two-year cabinet office holders (eligible to Commons), commanders-in-chief, thanked military commanders, governors-general, ten-year colonial governors, permanent civil servants with ten years in high offices, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer offices with concrete public/legal/military responsibility as qualifying criteria. Exclude scientific and literary eminence unconnected with politics because they are disputable and invite partisan selection. Time-in-office conditions prevent purely titular appointments and ensure practical experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reform path: aggregate qualified elements into the existing second chamber (life peers/representative peers)
rubrics_metrics.description: It might be feasible to aggregate the classes or categories just spoken of to the existing body in the character of peers for life. An ulterior step might be that the hereditary peerage be present by their representatives instead of personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reform can adapt legacy institutions by adding life peers chosen from qualified categories and using representative peers (e.g., one representative per ten peers chosen by the peerage) to broaden representation without wholesale abolition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-peer election method (adaptation of Mr. Hare's plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: All peers who were candidates ... enter names in a list. Peers vote (in person or by proxy) each for one. Every candidate with as many as ten votes is elected. If any one had more, all but ten may withdraw or ten selected by lot. Repeat until as many peers as possible are represented; small remainders handled specially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method aims to let peers choose representatives so that each representative actually represents a constituency within the peerage; non-elected peers compensated by eligibility to the Commons. Procedural detail designed to avoid domination by the majority in the peerage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Chamber elected by first (once removed) is a feasible alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Another possible mode ... would be to have it elected by the First; subject to the restriction that they should not nominate any of their own members. Such an assembly, emanating ... from popular choice only once removed, would not be considered to clash with democratic institutions ... be peculiarly unlikely to excite jealousy ... and would probably comprise many highly capable men unwilling to seek popular suffrage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second chamber chosen by the popular house (but excluding its own sitting members) can produce a less partisan, competent body that avoids direct conflict with the popular assembly while providing experience and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align departmental structure with subject-matter and avoid overlapping independent authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification of functionaries should correspond to that of subjects, and there should not be several departments independent of one another, to superintend different parts of the same natural whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a single objective (e.g., an efficient army) authority and resources should be unified under one control; divided independent authorities turn means into ends and sacrifice overall purpose to departmental self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear individual responsibility for executive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every executive function ... should be the appointed duty of some given individual. It should be apparent to all the world who did every thing, and through whose default any thing was left undone. Responsibility is null when nobody knows who is responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign single accountable officers to functions so praise and blame are not diluted; public visibility of responsibility increases effectiveness and deterrence against negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid boards for executive business because they obscure responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards ... are screens. What 'the Board' does is the act of nobody, and nobody can be made to answer for it. The Board suffers only in its collective character; and no individual member feels this further than his disposition leads him to identify his own estimation with that of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boards only when giving full discretionary power to a single official would be worse; otherwise prefer single heads with advisory counselors to preserve accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide professional advisers and consultative councils to ministers, especially in technical departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional advisers must therefore be provided for him. ... military and naval ministers ... should be provided with a Council, composed ... of able and experienced professional men. As a means of obtaining the best men ... they ought to be permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers are often general politicians lacking technical expertise; permanent councils of professionals (not removable with each ministry) ensure continuity, technical competence, and institutional memory. High appointments by selection should often be for fixed terms to prevent patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Councils should be consultative with recorded opinions; ultimate decision remains with the minister
rubrics_metrics.description: The councils should be consultative merely, in this sense, that the ultimate decision should rest undividedly with the minister himself; ... it ought to be impossible for [advisers] not to express an opinion, and impossible for him not to listen to and consider their recommendations ... every member ... is expected to give an opinion ... if there is a difference ... record the reasons of his opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make advisers formally accountable by requiring recorded opinions and reasons; the minister may override but individual records show who advised what, preserving responsibility and informing parliamentary or public scrutiny (exemplified by the Governor-General councils in India).

rubrics_metrics.name: High non-competitive appointments should be for fixed terms and not necessarily removable for political reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a good rule that all who hold high appointments to which they have risen by selection, and not by the ordinary course of promotion, should retain their office only for a fixed term, unless reappointed ... This rule renders appointments somewhat less likely to be jobbed ... and affords a means ... of getting rid of those who are least worth keeping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed-term tenure for selected high posts reduces patronage, allows performance-based replacement without scandal, and opens room for talented younger appointees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive officers should not be appointed by popular election
rubrics_metrics.description: A most important principle ... is that no executive functionaries should be appointed by popular election, neither by the votes of the people themselves, nor by those of their representatives. The entire business of government is skilled employment; the qualifications ... can not be properly judged of except by persons who have themselves some share of those qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selections for skilled public employment should rely on professional assessment and ministerial responsibility; popular elections politicize appointments and produce poor selection quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointing authority should have sole power of removal for subordinate officers (subject to misconduct exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: All subordinate public officers who are not appointed by some mode of public competition should be selected on the direct responsibility of the minister under whom they serve. The functionary who appoints should be the sole person empowered to remove any subordinate officer who is liable to removal, which the far greater number ought not to be, except for personal misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate appointment and removal power to preserve ministerial responsibility while protecting career civil service from arbitrary dismissal; most subordinate officials should have protection from removal except for proven misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head of executive in a republic: prefer appointment by representative body to popular election
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems far better that the chief magistrate in a republic should be appointed avowedly, as the chief minister in a constitutional monarchy is virtually, by the representative body. ... The President of the United States ... is almost always either an obscure man, or one who has gained any reputation he may possess in some other field than politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular election for head of state encourages electioneering, promotes less eminent candidates, and makes continuous campaigning central to public life. Appointing by the legislature (or appointing but with fixed term) tends to produce more eminent, politically tested leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countervailing mechanisms to avoid deadlock: fixed tenure plus dissolution power or ability to call new Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: He might, though appointed by Parliament, hold his office for a fixed period, independent of a Parliamentary vote ... or he could have the power to dissolve the House and appeal to the people ... There ought not to be any possibility of that deadlock in politics which would ensue on a quarrel ... neither of whom ... would have any legal means of ridding itself of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid paralysis or coups, provide constitutional means to resolve disputes between executive and legislature: fixed terms combined with dissolution power, or the executive's ability to call new elections, serve as safety valves. The power to call a new Parliament is important to test which party commands a majority and prevent prolonged interregna.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial officers should not be appointed by popular election; impartiality demands insulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all officers of government, those in whose appointment any participation of popular suffrage is the most objectionable are judicial officers. ... there are none in whose case absolute impartiality, and freedom from connection with politicians or sections of politicians, are of any thing like equal importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular election or direct political control over judges risks politicization and undermines impartiality. While irremovability has its own evils, public election/removal powers for judges are particularly detrimental because lay opinion cannot reliably judge professional judicial qualifications.
